title: The True Story Behind 'Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death'
author: Barry Levitt
body:
“A day natty is a day wasted.”

That’s the motto of Tony Huge, a prominent figure in the looksmaxxing community. In Huge’s lingo, “natty” means “natural,” as in refraining from using a heavy regimen of supplements popular in the rapidly growing online subculture of men that promotes extreme measures to maximize the potential of one’s physical appearance. Especially popular among young adults and teenagers, looksmaxxing often includes risky behavior like the use of trenbolone, a steroid designed to promote muscle growth in livestock that’s illegal for human use in the United States, and DNP, a toxic fertilizer that can burn fat but brings the potential for deadly side effects. For looksmaxxers, the goal is to achieve peak physical form to become more powerful and attractive to women—life expectancy be damned.

Filmmaker Stacey Lee first met Huge in late 2024, when looksmaxxing was still “a very fringe movement.” She was embarking on a project about the phenomenon, which she says has moved “to center stage” between then and the Nov. 10 release of her three-part series Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death, streaming on Hulu and Disney+.

The idea of injecting yourself with dangerous substances to become more muscular, or engaging in bone smashing—repeatedly striking your facial bones with blunt instruments in hopes your bones will heal thicker and stronger—may sound horrifying to most. But Lee understands the appeal. “It begins with a basic human need we all have, no matter our gender, for connection and belonging, and to be seen and respected. I think everyone can relate to the idea that we want to be the best version of ourselves,” she says.

But the goalposts move, and then move again. “You find yourself never being able to feel complete,” she says. You might achieve a buff physique or a bigger jawline, but ”these are superficial solutions to very deep and complex problems.”

Get Huge chronicles the rise of Tony Huge and the growing community of looksmaxxing. Along the way, it appears to brush up against true crime, as Lee delves into a string of unexplained deaths in the community.

The rise of a looksmaxxer

Tony Huge, a former bankruptcy lawyer, founded Enhanced Athlete in 2013 as a brand and YouTube channel. It was there that he first discussed experimenting with anabolic compounds, Selective Androgen Receptor Modulators (SARMs), and other techniques to build muscle. In 2016, he expanded Enhanced Athlete to include a supplement company that also sold unapproved performance-enhancing drugs.. The company was raided by the FDA following the launch of a criminal investigation alleging the manufacturing and distribution of unapproved SARMs and other chemicals. Its CEO, Scott Cavell, was arrested for selling fertilizer as an enhancement and went to prison for three years. Huge, Enhanced Athlete’s co-founder and brand ambassador, was not indicted. He soon moved to Pattaya, Thailand, where the drug laws are considerably more relaxed.

“Tony has this aura of radical transparency,” says Lee. “But it’s very controlled. He’s got an incredible way of working within gray areas. He’s managed to create a business and lifestyle that allows him to live on the very edge within the realms of the law—at least in Thailand.”

From Pattaya, Huge established a considerable fandom as a looksmaxxer. Though his once-popular YouTube channel has been banned since 2023, he still has nearly 175,000 followers on Instagram. “Tony offered community. He offered a father figure. He offered a blueprint for his life that had never been offered before,” says Lee. His sex life is also central to his appeal. “He’s got anywhere between eight and 10 girlfriends at any point in time, and the house is run by them,” explains Lee. “They make his food, get his supplements ready, do his laundry, and clean his house.”

That combination was enticing to Elon Muskular, one of the subjects Lee interviews in the docuseries. Before coming across Tony, Muskular had been depressed and disconnected. He started messaging Tony to express his admiration, before Tony invited him to move to Thailand, live with him, and run his marketing. Muskular dropped out of school and made the move. “He finds people at rock bottom, who don’t have anything to lose,” Muskular says of Huge in the docuseries. Muskular fell out with Huge over differing views and concerns over Huge’s treatment of other looksmaxxers, and the two no longer work together.

Trouble in paradise

Leo Longevity also counted himself as an admirer of Tony. The self-proclaimed biohacker became well known online for his videos about penis enhancement. In 2022, Leo moved to Thailand to live at Tony’s compound so the two could make videos together as part of the content creation aspect of both of their businesses. Once Huge and Leo got into a groove of creating together, they would publish several videos on YouTube everyday, a nearly unmatchable rate for competitors. The two became incredibly close friends, but the pressure to live up to expectations weighed heavily.

“In the biohacking/looksmaxxing space, the motivation towards extremes is because you always have to create a new precedent,” says Lee. “Back in the day, Tony was the most controversial guy on the internet, and now he’s looking at what other looksmaxxers would do. He’s like, ‘I got to keep up with this.’”

It was against this backdrop of immense pressure that tragedy struck. Leo and Huge’s relationship began to feel strained. There was a struggle for power, as both men wanted to be the dominant alpha in their videos, and each had his own ideas about how to achieve those goals. There was also a new protegé in place in Connor Murphy, a rising star on the looksmaxxing scene who joined the duo in Pattaya at the beginning of 2023. The series suggests that Tony was infatuated with Connor, which infuriated Leo. According to Get Huge, on Jan. 27, 2023, Leo began to isolate himself. He was found dead three days later in a bathroom in Huge’s house.

Leo Longevity’s autopsy report, according to sources close to Pattaya police, indicates that his fatal injuries were caused by another person. The investigation into his death remains open, and no suspect has been identified. Huge has denied any involvement.

A history of suspicious deaths and disappearances

Get Huge rewinds the story to shed light on another tragic death that took place in Huge’s circle years earlier. Super Beast, Tony’s former chemist, says in the docuseries that Nick Weisser, a close friend of Huge’s and his IT guy, had regular falling-outs with his friend and boss. Super Beast recalls that Weisser attempted to blackmail Huge, threatening to leak critical information about Enhanced, and was found dead a couple of weeks later.

Josh Brooks, a fellow looksmaxxer who Huge describes as a “best friend” in the docuseries, was another of his protegés. Brooks, Super Beast explains in the series, also tried to blackmail Tony, and took his mentor’s business branding and tried to slightly alter it and pass it off as his own. In 2021, there was a fire in Brooks' apartment in Colombia, and he fell out of the window to his death.

In 2022, Coach Trevor, another of Huge’s close friends, disappeared. “I personally don’t know what happened to him. None of us do,” Super Beast remarks in Get Huge. In 2024, Scott Cavell, the CEO of Enhanced Athlete, was found dead in a hotel. An official cause of death hasn’t been released, though Super Beast says he believes that Cavell was killed. “Scott did drugs. He wouldn’t do the amount that killed him,” he says. He does stop short of making accusations for who is responsible for any of these deaths and disappearances. (Huge has not been declared a suspect.) But he has plenty to say about Huge’s empire: “It’s not a brotherhood. It’s a gathering point for weak-minded people. They don’t take care of each other. They don’t uplift each other. They find ways to f-ck each other’s lives up. Basically a cyclone.”

Filming for Get Huge wrapped in June of 2026—until a new development brought the team back into production. On July 7, Connor Murphy died by drowning in the lake in his backyard in Thailand. He had been exhibiting increasingly erratic behavior, including claiming that he was gaining superpowers after injecting gold into his bloodstream. As of the docuseries’ release, Murphy’s death is believed to be an accident.

How far can looksmaxxing go?

While Get Huge investigates the deaths of Leo Longevity and others connected to Tony Huge, it’s also a broader look at the rise of the looksmaxxing movement itself. In one scene, Huge travels to Las Vegas for a bodybuilding show, where he meets a group of teens as young as 13. Concerned with the decrease in brand awareness as younger looksmaxxers like Clavicular and Androgenic increase their share of the fandom, he appears to be looking to increase his reach to younger audiences. “Tony doesn’t have the same gravitas with the next generation, and that leads him to Vegas to try and figure out how to capture a piece of that pie,” says Lee. Just moments into their conversation, one of them asks if Huge can get them steroids. He laughs off the question, but it lingers.

“The challenge of this experimental biohacking culture,” says Lee, “is that our bodies are all very different. One thing that works for Tony Huge might not work for the 16-year-old kid in Iowa who just wants to get jacked.” There’s also no need for any of these looksmaxxers to verify that they’re actually taking what they’re claiming. Clavicular, currently the most popular looksmaxxer, says he does meth to help maintain his physique. “He may not be taking what he’s saying he’s taking, and this kid who’s using it as a blueprint for his life doesn’t have the discernment to know that,” Lee says.

Safeguards implemented by social media platforms, including Huge’s YouTube ban, have played a role in his decreasing reach. But he and other looksmaxxers decry these removals as censorship. And Lee understands that anything that’s perceived as censorship “can get weaponized,” using Andrew Tate as an example. “Every time he gets censored, he uses it as part of his argument, and it galvanizes more followers,” says Lee. “If they get kicked off YouTube, they go to Rumble, they go to 4Chan. Whatever the most underground forum is.”

Lee holds out some hope that the rise of looksmaxxing might be curbed. “I think what we’re witnessing now is a dismantling of these power structures of masculinity and more of a reckoning. The Tate brothers are on trial, and you’re seeing a turning of the tide politically.”

What does concern Lee is the rising use of AI in looksmaxxing. Her series shows that Tony’s team regularly produces and creates content using AI. “Even if Tony’s not around, he can live forever on the internet using those tools,” she says.

Adds Lee: “If the humans stop, do the machines carry it on?”
